title: Great Classroom Management With Your Eyes Closed https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2026/07/17/visualization-great-classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that visualization is an underused but powerful classroom management tool, especially useful during summer break when teachers can reflect with fresh eyes. His central claim is that good behavior does not materialize out of thin air: unless a teacher can clearly picture what an excellent classroom looks and feels like, they will never build one. He recounts using visualization himself when creating SCM, mentally rehearsing his ideal classroom from students entering the room through dismissal, scene by scene, before recreating it in real life. The concrete technique he teaches is a closed-eye rehearsal practice: envision your dream class in specific, sequential detail (how students enter, where they put backpacks, how routines unfold) across several sessions until the picture is fully clear, then teach that vision to students and hold everyone accountable to it. He notes that visualized time moves much faster than real time and that with practice a teacher can mentally run through an entire day in just a few minutes.
points: Visualization works because it clarifies exactly what you want your classroom to look like before you try to build it.
Rehearse your ideal day scene by scene, from students entering the room to dismissal, as if watching a movie play out.
Everyone's dream classroom looks different, so use the exercise to build your own vision, not someone else's.
With practice, a ten-minute routine can be visualized in about 30 seconds, making the exercise fast to repeat often.
The strategies and principles needed to build the visualized classroom already exist in the SCM archive, books, and YouTube channel.
quotes: You see, if you don’t know what you want and what it looks like, then you’ll never achieve exceptional classroom management. Good behavior doesn’t materialize out of thin air.
My method when I was first creating SCM was to visualize what I wanted in my mind’s eye first. I viewed my perfect classroom from start to finish.

I saw them gently hang up their coats, align their backpacks behind their chairs, check their mailboxes, place their homework in the top right-hand corner of their desks, and immediately begin the daily grammar work.
Once the picture was clear, I went about recreating it in the classroom. This is how SCM was born. Envision what you want. Teach it to your students. Hold them and you accountable for its execution.
For me, I visualize a ten-minute beginning-of-day routine in about 30 seconds.
You get better the more you do it, but you should be able to “see” your day from start to finish in just a few minutes.
Work on it for several or more closed-eye sessions this summer until you have a clear representation of what you want.
